entries.6e66467017ed182c21ae566575fdb62de925f2de: <div sID="gen4445" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="18" osisID="Josh.18" sID="Josh.18"/> <div eID="gen4445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4446" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4447" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The setting up of the tabernacle at Shiloh, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. The stirring up of the seven tribes that were yet unsettled to look after their lot, and the putting of them in a method for it, by Joshua, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.2-Josh.18.7">ver. 2-7</reference>. III. The distributing of the land into seven lots, by certain men employed for that purpose, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.8-Josh.18.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>. IV. The determining of these seven portions to the seven tribes yet unprovided for by lot, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.10">ver. 10</reference>. V. The particular lot of the tribe of Benjamin, the borders of it, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.11-Josh.18.20">ver. 11-20</reference>. And the cities contained in it, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.21-Josh.18.28">ver. 21-28</reference>. The other six tribes we shall find well provided for in the <div eID="gen4447" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4446" type="introduction"/>
entries.0cb4e29418e418686b60c74f2c78560337636a6c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9"/><title type="x-s3">The Tabernacle at Shiloh. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1444.)</title> <div sID="gen4448" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the whole congregation of the children of Israel assembled together at Shiloh, and set up the tabernacle of the congregation there. And the land was subdued before them. <div eID="gen4448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4449" type="x-p"/> In the midst of the story of the dividing of the land comes in this account of the setting up of the tabernacle, which had hitherto continued in its old place in the centre of their camp; but now that three of the four squadrons that used to surround it in the wilderness were broken and diminished, those of Judah, Ephraim, and Reuben, by the removal of those tribes to their respective possessions, and that of Dan only remained entire, it was time to think of removing the tabernacle itself into a city. Many a time the priests and Levites had taken it down, carried it, and set it up again in the wilderness, according to the directions given them (<reference osisRef="Num.4.5-Num.4.33">Num. iv. 5</reference>, &c.); but now they must do it for good and all, not one of the stakes thereof must any more be removed, nor any of the cords thereof broken, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.20">Isa. xxxiii. 20</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen4449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4450" type="x-p"/> I. The place to which the tabernacle was removed, and in which it was set up. It was <hi type="italic">Shiloh,</hi> a city in the lot of Ephraim, but lying close upon the lot of Benjamin. Doubtless God himself did some way or other direct them to this place, for he had promised to <hi type="italic">choose the place</hi> where he would make <hi type="italic">his name to dwell,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.12.11">Deut. xii. 11</reference>. It is most probable God made known his mind in this matter by the judgment of Urim. This place was pitched upon, 1. Because it was in the heart of the country, nearer the centre than Jerusalem was, and therefore the more convenient for the meeting of all Israel there from the several parts of the country; it had been in the midst of their camp in the wilderness, and therefore must now be in the midst of their nation, as that which sanctified the whole, and was <hi type="italic">the glory in the midst of them.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Ps.46.5">Ps. xlvi. 5</reference>. 2. Because it was in the lot of that tribe of which Joshua was, who was now their chief magistrate, and it would be both for his honour and convenience and for the advantage of the country to have it near him. The testimony of Israel and the thrones of judgment do well together, <reference osisRef="Ps.122.4-Ps.122.5">Ps. cxxii. 4, 5</reference>. 3. Some think there was an eye to the name of the place, <hi type="italic">Shiloh</hi> being the name by which the Messiah was known in dying Jacob's prophecy (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen. xlix. 10</reference>), which prophecy, no doubt, was well known among the Jews; the setting up of the tabernacle in Shiloh gave them a hint that in that Shiloh whom Jacob spoke of all the ordinances of this worldly sanctuary should have their accomplishment in a greater and more perfect tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.1">Heb. ix. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.11">11</reference>. And Dr. Lightfoot thinks that the place where the tabernacle was set up was therefore called <hi type="italic">Shiloh,</hi> because of the peaceableness of the land at this time; as afterwards in Salem was his temple, which also signifies <hi type="italic">peaceable.</hi> <div eID="gen4450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4451" type="x-p"/> II. The solemn manner of doing it: <hi type="italic">The whole congregation assembled together</hi> to attend the solemnity, to do honour to the ark of God, as the token of his presence, and to bid it welcome to its settlement. Every Israelite was interested in it, and therefore all testified their joy and satisfaction upon this occasion. See <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.15">2 Sam. vi. 15</reference>. It is probable those tribes that were yet encamped when the tabernacle was removed to Shiloh decamped from Gilgal and pitched about Shiloh, for every true Israelite will desire to fix where God's tabernacle fixed. Mention is made, on this occasion, of the land being subdued before them, to intimate that the country, hereabouts at least, being thoroughly reduced, they met with no opposition, nor were they apprehensive of any danger, but thought it time to make this grateful acknowledgment of God's goodness to them in the constant series of successes with which he had blessed them. It was a good presage of a comfortable settlement to themselves in Canaan, when their first care was to see the ark well settled as soon as they had a safe place ready to settle it in. Here the ark continued about 300 years, till the sins of Eli's house forfeited the ark, lost it and ruined Shiloh, and its ruins were long after made use of as warnings to Jerusalem. <hi type="italic">Go, see what I did to Shiloh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.7.12">Jer. vii. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.60">Ps. lxxviii. 60</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9"/> <div eID="gen4451" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Joshua Reproves the Unsettled Tribes. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1444.)</title> <div sID="gen4452" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super"></hi> <hi type="super">2</hi> And there remained among the children of Israel seven tribes, which had not yet received their inheritance. <hi type="super">3</hi> And Joshua said unto the children of Israel, How long <hi type="italic">are</hi> ye slack to go to possess the land, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of your fathers hath given you? <hi type="super">4</hi> Give out from among you three men for <hi type="italic">each</hi> tribe: and I will send them, and they shall rise, and go through the land, and describe it according to the inheritance of them; and they shall come <hi type="italic">again</hi> to me. <hi type="super">5</hi> And they shall divide it into seven parts: Judah shall abide in their coast on the south, and the house of Joseph shall abide in their coasts on the north. <hi type="super">6</hi> Ye shall therefore describe the land <hi type="italic">into</hi> seven parts, and bring <hi type="italic">the description</hi> hither to me, that I may cast lots for you here before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God. <hi type="super">7</hi> But the Levites have no part among you; for the priesthood of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> their inheritance: and Gad, and Reuben, and half the tribe of Manasseh, have received their inheritance beyond Jordan on the east, which Moses the servant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> gave them. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the men arose, and went away: and Joshua charged them that went to describe the land, saying, Go and walk through the land, and describe it, and come again to me, that I may here cast lots for you before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in Shiloh. <hi type="super">9</hi> And the men went and passed through the land, and described it by cities into seven parts in a book, and came <hi type="italic">again</hi> to Joshua to the host at Shiloh. <hi type="super">10</hi> And Joshua cast lots for them in Shiloh before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and there Joshua divided the land unto the children of Israel according to their divisions. <div eID="gen4452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4453" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Joshua reproves those tribes which were yet unsettled that they did not bestir themselves to gain a settlement in the land which God had given them. Seven tribes were yet unprovided for, though sure of an inheritance, yet uncertain where it should be, and it seems in no great care about it, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.2">v. 2</reference>. And with them Joshua reasons (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">How long are you slack?</hi> 1. They were too well pleased with their present condition, liked well enough to live in a body together, the more the merrier, and, like the Babel-builders, had no mind to be scattered abroad and break good company. The spoil of the cities they had taken served them to live plentifully upon for the present, and they banished the thoughts of time to come. Perhaps the tribes of Judah and Joseph, who had already received their inheritance in the countries next adjoining, were generous in entertaining their brethren who were yet unprovided for, so that they went from one good house to another among their friends, with which, instead of grudging that they were postponed, they were so well pleased that they cared not for going to houses of their own. 2. They were slothful and dilatory. It may be they wished the thing done, but had not spirit to stir in it, or move towards the doing of it, though it was so much for their own advantage; like the sluggard, that <hi type="italic">hides his hand in his bosom, and it grieves him to bring it to his mouth again.</hi> The countries that remained to be divided lay at a distance, and some parts of them in the hands of the Canaanites. If they go to take possession of them, the cities must be rebuilt or repaired, they must drive their flocks and herds a great way, and carry their wives and children to strange places, and this will not be done without care and pains, and breaking through some hardships; thus <hi type="italic">he that observes the wind shall not sow, and he that regards the clouds shall not reap,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.4">Eccl. xi. 4</reference>. Note, Many are diverted from real duties, and debarred from real comforts, by seeming difficulties. God by his grace has given us a title to a good land, the heavenly Canaan, but we are <hi type="italic">slack to take possession;</hi> we enter not into that rest, as we might by faith, and hope, and holy joy; we live not in heaven, as we might by setting our affections on things above and having our conversation there. How long shall it be thus with us? How long shall we thus stand in our own light, and <hi type="italic">forsake our own mercies</hi> for lying vanities? Joshua was sensible of the inconveniences of this delay, that, while they neglected to take possession of the land that was conquered, the Canaanites were recovering strength and spirit, and fortifying themselves in the places that were yet in their hands, which would make the total expulsion of them the more difficult. They would lose their advantages by not following their blow; and therefore, <hi type="italic">as an eagle stirreth up her nest,</hi> so Joshua stirs them up to take possession of their lot. He is ready to do his part, if they will but do theirs. <div eID="gen4453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4454" type="x-p"/> II. He puts them in a way to settle themselves. <div eID="gen4454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4455" type="x-p"/> 1. The land that remained must be surveyed, an account taken of the cities, and the territories belonging to them, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.4">v. 4</reference>. These must be divided into seven equal parts, as near as they could guess at their true value, which they must have an eye to, and not merely to the number of the cities and extent of the country. Judah is fixed on the south and Joseph on the north of Shiloh, to protect the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.5">v. 5</reference>), and therefore they need not describe their country, but those countries only that were yet undisposed of. He gives a reason (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.7">v. 7</reference>) why they must divide it into seven parts only, because the Levites were to have no temporal estate (as we say), but their benefices only, which were entailed upon their families: <hi type="italic">The priesthood of the Lord is their inheritance,</hi> and a very honourable, comfortable, plentiful inheritance it was. Gad and Reuben, with half of the tribe of Manasseh, were already fixed, and needed not to have any further care taken of them. Now, (1.) The surveyors were three men out of each of the seven tribes that were to be provided for (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.4">v. 4</reference>), one-and-twenty in all, who perhaps for greater expedition, because they had already lost time, divided themselves into three companies, one of each tribe in each company, and took each their district to survey. The matter was thus referred equally, that there might be neither any partiality used in making up the seven lots, nor any shadow of suspicion given, but all might be satisfied that they had right done them. (2.) The survey was accordingly made, and brought in to Joshua, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.8-Josh.18.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. Josephus says it was seven months in the doing. And we must in it observe, [1.] The faith and courage of the persons employed: abundance of Canaanites remained in the land, and all raging against Israel, <hi type="italic">as a bear robbed of her whelps;</hi> the business of these surveyors would soon be known, and what could they expect but to be way-laid, and have their brains knocked out by the fierce observers? But in obedience to Joshua's command, and in dependence upon God's power, they thus put their lives in their hands to serve their country. [2.] The good providence of God in protecting them from the many deaths they were exposed to, and bringing them all safely again to the host at Shiloh. When we are in the way of our duty we are under the special protection of the Almighty. <div eID="gen4455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4456" type="x-p"/> 2. When it was surveyed, and reduced to seven lots, then Joshua would, by appeal to God, and direction from him, determine which of these lots should belong to each tribe (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">That I may cast lots for you here</hi> at the tabernacle (because it was a sacred transaction) <hi type="italic">before the Lord our God,</hi> to whom each tribe must have an eye, with thankfulness for the conveniences and submission to the inconveniences of their allotment. What we have in the world we must acknowledge God's property in, and dispose of it as before him, with justice, and charity, and dependence upon Providence. The heavenly Canaan is described to us in a book, the book of the scriptures, and there are in it mansions and portions sufficient for all God's spiritual Israel. Christ is our Joshua that divides it to us. On him we must attend, and to him we must apply for an inheritance with the saints in light. See <reference osisRef="John.17.2-John.17.3">John xvii. 2, 3</reference>.
entries.efc3a32141f50852a2e2e00d4973c790d29e6a5b: <div eID="gen4456" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Lot of Benjamin. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1444.)</title> <div sID="gen4457" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super"></hi> <hi type="super">11</hi> And the lot of the tribe of the children of Benjamin came up according to their families: and the coast of their lot came forth between the children of Judah and the children of Joseph. <hi type="super">12</hi> And their border on the north side was from Jordan; and the border went up to the side of Jericho on the north side, and went up through the mountains westward; and the goings out thereof were at the wilderness of Beth-aven. <hi type="super">13</hi> And the border went over from thence toward Luz, to the side of Luz, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Beth-el, southward; and the border descended to Ataroth-adar, near the hill that <hi type="italic">lieth</hi> on the south side of the nether Beth-horon. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the border was drawn <hi type="italic">thence,</hi> and compassed the corner of the sea southward, from the hill that <hi type="italic">lieth</hi> before Beth-horon southward; and the goings out thereof were at Kirjath-baal, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Kirjath-jearim, a city of the children of Judah: this <hi type="italic">was</hi> the west quarter. <hi type="super">15</hi> And the south quarter <hi type="italic">was</hi> from the end of Kirjath-jearim, and the border went out on the west, and went out to the well of waters of Nephtoah: <hi type="super">16</hi> And the border came down to the end of the mountain that <hi type="italic">lieth</hi> before the valley of the son of Hinnom, <hi type="italic">and</hi> which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the valley of the giants on the north, and descended to the valley of Hinnom, to the side of Jebusi on the south, and descended to En-rogel, <hi type="super">17</hi> And was drawn from the north, and went forth to En-shemesh, and went forth toward Geliloth, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> over against the going up of Adummim, and descended to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben, <hi type="super">18</hi> And passed along toward the side over against Arabah northward, and went down unto Arabah: <hi type="super">19</hi> And the border passed along to the side of Beth-hoglah northward: and the outgoings of the border were at the north bay of the salt sea at the south end of Jordan: this <hi type="italic">was</hi> the south coast. <hi type="super">20</hi> And Jordan was the border of it on the east side. This <hi type="italic">was</hi> the inheritance of the children of Benjamin, by the coasts thereof round about, according to their families. <hi type="super">21</hi> Now the cities of the tribe of the children of Benjamin according to their families were Jericho, and Beth-hoglah, and the valley of Keziz, <hi type="super">22</hi> And Beth-arabah, and Zemaraim, and Beth-el, <hi type="super">23</hi> And Avim, and Parah, and Ophrah, <hi type="super">24</hi> And Chephar-haammonai, and Ophni, and Gaba; twelve cities with their villages: <hi type="super">25</hi> Gibeon, and Ramah, and Beeroth, <hi type="super">26</hi> And Mizpeh, and Chephirah, and Mozah, <hi type="super">27</hi> And Rekem, and Irpeel, and Taralah, <hi type="super">28</hi> And Zelah, Eleph, and Jebusi, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Jerusalem, Gibeath, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Kirjath; fourteen cities with their villages. This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the inheritance of the children of Benjamin according to their families. <div eID="gen4457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4458" type="x-p"/> We have here the lot of the tribe of Benjamin, which Providence cast next to Joseph on the one hand, because Benjamin was own and only brother to Joseph, and was little Benjamin (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.27">Ps. lxviii. 27</reference>), that needed the protection of great Joseph, and yet had a better protector, for <hi type="italic">the Lord shall cover him all the day long,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.33.12">Deut. xxxiii. 12</reference>. And it was next to Judah on the other hand, that this tribe might hereafter unite with Judah in an adherence to the throne of David and the temple at Jerusalem. Here we have, 1. The exact borders and limits of this tribe, which we need not be exact in the explication of. As it had Judah on the south and Joseph on the north, so it had Jordan on the east and Dan on the west. The western border is said to <hi type="italic">compass the corner of the sea southward</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.14">v. 14</reference>), whereas no part of the lot of this tribe came near to the great sea. Bishop Patrick thinks the meaning is that it ran along in a parallel line to the great sea, though at a distance. Dr. Fuller suggests that since it is not called <hi type="italic">the great sea,</hi> but only <hi type="italic">the sea,</hi> which often signifies any lake or mere, it may be meant of the pool of Gibeon, which may be called <hi type="italic">a corner</hi> or <hi type="italic">canton</hi> of the sea; it is called the <hi type="italic">great waters of Gibeon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.41.12">Jer. xli. 12</reference>), and it is compassed by the western border of this tribe. 2. The particular cities in this tribe, not all, but the most considerable. Twenty-six are here named. Jericho is put first, though dismantled, and forbidden to be rebuilt as a city with gates and walls, because it might be built and inhabited as a country village, and so was not useless to this tribe. Gilgal, where Israel first encamped when Saul was made king (<reference osisRef="1Sam.11.15">1 Sam. xi. 15</reference>), was in this tribe. It was afterwards a very profane place. <reference osisRef="Hos.9.15">Hos. ix. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">All their wickedness is in Gilgal.</hi> Beth-el was in this tribe, a famous place. Though Benjamin adhered to the house of David, yet Beth-el, it seems, was in the possession of the house of Joseph (<reference osisRef="Judg.1.23-Judg.1.25">Judg. i. 23-25</reference>), and there Jeroboam set up one of his calves. In this tribe was Gibeon, where the altar was in the beginning of Solomon's time, <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.3">2 Chron. i. 3</reference>. Gibeah likewise, that infamous place where the Levite's concubine was abused. Mizpeh, and near it Samuel's Ebenezer, and also Anathoth, Jeremiah's city, were in this tribe, as was the northern part of Jerusalem. Paul was the honour of this tribe (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.1">Rom. xi. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.5">Phil. iii. 5</reference>); but where his land lay we know not: he sought the better country.  <chapter eID="Josh.18"/> <div eID="gen4458" type="x-p"/>

entries.0d96e310d52a6de9f3de99936ff092e3a316b47c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2144"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 18</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.18.1">Jos 18:1</reference>. The Tabernacle Set Up at Shiloh.</title> <div sID="gen2886" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2144"/><hi type="bold">1. the whole congregation ... assembled together at Shiloh--</hi>The main body of the Israelites had been diminished by the separation of the three tribes, Judah, Ephraim, and Manasseh into their respective allotments; and the country having been in a great measure subdued, the camp was removed to Shiloh (now Seilun). It was twenty or twenty-five miles north of Jerusalem, twelve north of Beth-el, and ten south of Shechem, and embosomed in a rugged and romantic glen. This sequestered spot in the heart of the country might have been recommended by the dictates of convenience. There the allotment of the territory could be most conveniently made, north, south, east, and west, to the different tribes. But "the tabernacle of the congregation was also set up there," and its removal therefore must have been made or sanctioned by divine intimation (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.11">De 12:11</reference>). It remained in Shiloh for more than three hundred years (<reference osisRef="1Sam.4.1-1Sam.4.11">1Sa 4:1-11</reference>). <div eID="gen2886" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa643bd49a4e1dc69fcc09c14f0e603d44a0c2eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2145"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.18.2-Josh.18.9">Jos 18:2-9</reference>. The Remainder of the Land Described.</title> <div sID="gen2887" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2145"/><hi type="bold">2. there remained ... seven tribes, which had not yet received their inheritance--</hi>The selection of Shiloh for the seat of worship, together with the consequent removal of the camp thither, had necessarily interrupted the casting of lots, which was commenced by fixing localities for the tribes of Judah and Joseph. Various causes led to a long delay in resuming it. The satisfaction of the people with their change to so pleasant and fertile a district, their preference of a nomad life, a love of ease, and reluctance to renew the war, seem to have made them indifferent to the possession of a settled inheritance. But Joshua was too much alive to the duty laid on him by the Lord to let matters continue in that state; and accordingly, since a general conquest of the land had been made, he resolved to proceed immediately with the lot, believing that when each tribe should receive its inheritance, a new motive would arise to lead them to exert themselves in securing the full possession. <div eID="gen2887" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d1704c5eb6acf742b95b41bd2d9aef65ec26b2a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2146"/><div sID="gen2888" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2146"/><hi type="bold">3. How long are ye slack to go to possess the land, which the Lord God of your fathers hath given you--</hi>This reproof conveys an impression that the seven tribes were dilatory to a criminal extent. <div eID="gen2888" type="x-p"/>
entries.14a052010678443385bec77311db9c2b078bf3c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2147"/><div sID="gen2889" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2147"/><hi type="bold">4-9. Give out from among you three men for each tribe--</hi>Though the lot determined the part of the country where each tribe was to be located, it could not determine the extent of territory which might be required; and the dissatisfaction of the children of Joseph with the alleged smallness of their possession gave reason to fear that complaints might arise from other quarters, unless precautions were taken to make a proper distribution of the land. For this purpose a commission was given to twenty-one persons--three chosen from each of the seven tribes which had not yet received their inheritance, to make an accurate survey of the country. <div eID="gen2889" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f9f540065b3fe2c9348b402dd4e28fe4b8da2c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2149"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.18.10">Jos 18:10</reference>. Divided by Lot.</title> <div sID="gen2891" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2149"/><hi type="bold">10. Joshua cast lots for them in Shiloh before the Lord--</hi>before the tabernacle, where the divine presence was manifested, and which associated with the lot the idea of divine sanction. <div eID="gen2891" type="x-p"/>
entries.399d32a6a01b4e0bf6fafab53ccd7d697c2803de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2150"/><div sID="gen2892" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2150"/><hi type="bold">11. the lot of ... Benjamin came up--</hi>It has been supposed that there were two urns or vessels, from which the lots were drawn: one containing the names of the tribes, the other containing those of the seven portions; and that the two were drawn out simultaneously.<div eID="gen2892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the coast of their lot came forth between the children of Judah and the children of Joseph--</hi>Thus the prophecy of Moses respecting the inheritance of Benjamin was remarkably accomplished. (See on <reference osisRef="Deut.33.12">De 33:12</reference>). <chapter eID="Josh.18"/>

entries.1080c0cc9d09747f77d6bb14a7f672e6bcff517c: <div eID="gen8073" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen8074" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8075" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8075" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8074" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8076" type="x-p"/> The tabernacle is set up at Shiloh, <reference osisRef="Jos.18.1">Jos 18:1</reference>. Seven of the tribes having not yet received their inheritance, <reference osisRef="Jos.18.2">Jos 18:2</reference>. Joshua orders three men from each tribe to be chosen, and sent to examine the land and divide it into seven parts, which should be distributed among them by lot, <reference osisRef="Jos.18.3-Jos.18.7">Jos 18:3-7</reference>. The men go and do as commanded, and return to Joshua, <reference osisRef="Jos.18.8">Jos 18:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.18.9">Jos 18:9</reference>. Joshua casts lots for them, <reference osisRef="Jos.18.10">Jos 18:10</reference>. The lot of Benjamin, how situated, <reference osisRef="Jos.18.11">Jos 18:11</reference>. Its northern boundaries, <reference osisRef="Jos.18.12-Jos.18.14">Jos 18:12-14</reference>. Its southern boundaries, <reference osisRef="Jos.18.15-Jos.18.19">Jos 18:15-19</reference>. Its eastern boundary, <reference osisRef="Jos.18.20">Jos 18:20</reference>. Its cities, <reference osisRef="Jos.18.21-Jos.18.28">Jos 18:21-28</reference>. <div eID="gen8076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8077" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen8077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8078" type="x-p"/> Israel assembled together at Shiloh - This appears to have been a considerable town about fifteen miles from Jerusalem, in the tribe of Ephraim, and nearly in the center of the whole land. To this place both the camp of Israel, and the ark of the Lord, were removed from Gilgal, after a residence there of seven years. Here the tabernacle remained one hundred and thirty years, as is generally supposed, being the most conveniently situated for access to the different tribes, and for safety, the Israelites having possession of the land on all sides; for it is here added, the land was subdued before them - the Canaanites were so completely subdued, that there was no longer any general resistance to the Israelitish arms.
entries.23a3ec907fc638a454eb40f288243875048ce848: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen8078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8079" type="x-p"/> How long are ye slack to go to possess the land - We find an unaccountable backwardness in this people to enter on the inheritance which God had given them! They had so long been supported by miracle, without any exertions of their own, that they found it difficult to shake themselves from their inactivity. When it was necessary that all the people should go out to battle, they went with a measure of confidence, expecting miraculous help from God, and confiding in their numbers, but when each tribe found it necessary to fight for itself, in order to its establishment and the extension of its borders, it was discouraged, and chose rather a life of inglorious ease than the possession of an inheritance which would cost it much labor to conquer.
entries.827ab1e0296dd0ef6388e7e5fb5c1bffa24cf199: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen8079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8080" type="x-p"/> Three men for each tribe - Probably meaning only three from each of the seven tribes who had not yet received their inheritance. It is likely that these twenty-one men were accompanied by a military guard, for without this they might have been easily cut off by straggling parties of the Canaanites. <div eID="gen8080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8081" type="x-p"/> They shall - describe it - It is likely they were persons well acquainted with geography and mensuration, without which it would have been impossible for them to have divided the land in the way necessary on this occasion.
entries.4c5ca7c2f4db8aa43e24f6e9396ab52ba8833544: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen8081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8082" type="x-p"/> Judah shall abide - on the south, and the house of Joseph - on the north - Joshua does not mean that the tribe of Judah occupied the south, and the tribe of Ephraim and Manasseh the north of the promised land; this was not the fact: but being now at Shiloh, a considerable way in the territory of Ephraim, and not far from that of Judah, he speaks of them in relation to the place in which he then was. Calmet considers him as thus addressing the deputies: "Go and examine the whole of the country which remains yet to be possessed; do not take into consideration the tribe of Judah, which is on the south, nor the tribe of Ephraim, which is on the north of where we now are, but carefully divide the remaining land which is not occupied by these tribes into seven equal parts." This makes a very good sense, and frees the place from embarrassment.
entries.a7f37e9c64e49cb591d15b7d57e449d21e614a32: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen8082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8083" type="x-p"/> The priesthood of the Lord is their inheritance - We have already seen that the priests and Levites had the sacrifices, oblations tithes, first-fruits, redemption-money of the firstborn, etc., for their inheritance; they had no landed possessions in Israel; the Lord was their portion.
entries.b57cfe8bf22084d079c3e8e5ba8600f0ec215502: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen8083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8084" type="x-p"/> And described it in a book - This as far as I can recollect, is the first act of surveying on record. These men and their work differed widely from those who had searched the land in the time of Moses; they went only to discover the nature of the country, and the state of its inhabitants; but these went to take an actual geographical survey of it, in order to divide it among the tribes which had not yet received their portions. We may suppose that the country was exactly described in a book, that is, a map, pointing out the face of the country, accompanied with descriptions of each part.
entries.d8d10a123378292d48374b0ff3351c34f3b8ef6c: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen8084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8085" type="x-p"/> And the lot - of Benjamin came up - On the manner of casting the lot, see on <reference osisRef="Jos.14.2">Jos 14:2</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Num.26.55">Num 26:55</reference> (note). There were probably two urns, one of which contained the names of the seven tribes, and the other that of the seven portions. They therefore took out one name out of the first urn, and one portion out of the second, and thus the portion was adjudged to that tribe.
entries.b912975c74647a143f5fb2f00a920ae3e9b56872: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen8085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8086" type="x-p"/> The wilderness of Beth-aven - This was the same as Beth-el; but this name was not given to it till Jeroboam had fixed one of his golden calves there. Its first name signifies the house of God; its second, the house of iniquity.
entries.7b1b9b4b5e85e0bfe5064a04bf99d8ce077843c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen8086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8087" type="x-p"/> To the side of Jebusi - The mountain of Zion, that was near Jerusalem; for Jebusi, or Jebus, was the ancient name of this city.
entries.d4592d7c033df6fffeff2c33027a77a29c7ae1b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen8087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8088" type="x-p"/> En-shemesh - The fountain of the sun; a proof of the idolatrous nature of the ancient inhabitants of this land. <div eID="gen8088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8089" type="x-p"/> Geliloth - As the word signifies borders or limits, it is probably not the proper name of a place: And went forth towards the Borders which are over against the ascent to Adummim.
entries.889795db0550e03035b6f422e730132d9e93b7c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen8089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8090" type="x-p"/> The north bay of the Salt Sea - As the word לשון leshon signifies the tongue, it may here refer to the point of the Dead or Salt Sea. Of these tongues or points it had two, one on the north, and the other on the south.
entries.9759786ab4552f81fbc5c3148bd28a7fa820f4a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen8090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8091" type="x-p"/> Now the cities - Some of these cities have been mentioned before, and described; of others we know nothing but the name.
entries.8f1b041278c9b8e84f5d6db1b702ef403e64cd2e: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen8091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8092" type="x-p"/> And Gaba - Supposed to be the same as Gibeah of Saul, a place famous for having given birth to the first king of Israel; and infamous for the shocking act towards the Levite's wife, mentioned <reference osisRef="Jdg.19.16-Jdg.19.30">Jdg 19:16-30</reference>, which was the cause of a war in which the tribe of Benjamin was nearly exterminated. Judges 20:29-48.
entries.28db3747fc32eaeee2515f2cd912960be82e1b58: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen8092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8093" type="x-p"/> Gibeon - See before, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.1-Jos.10.14">Jos 10:1-14</reference> (note). This place is famous for the confederacy of the five kings against Israel, and their miraculous defeat. Ramah, a place about six or eight miles north of Jerusalem. Beeroth, i.e., wells; one of the four cities which belonged to the Gibeonites, who made peace with the Israelites by stratagem. See <reference osisRef="Jos.9.3-Jos.9.15">Jos 9:3-15</reference>.
entries.512f59ba7df76a5f9280a642780b6acfe3896d44: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen8093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8094" type="x-p"/> And Mizpeh - This place is celebrated in the sacred writings. Here the people were accustomed to assemble often in the presence of the Lord, as in the deliberation concerning the punishment to be inflicted on the men of Gibeah, for the abuse of the Levite's wife. <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.1-Jdg.20.3">Jdg 20:1-3</reference>. Samuel assembled the people here to exhort them to renounce their idolatry, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.5">1Sam 7:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.6">1Sam 7:6</reference>. In this same place Saul was chosen to be king, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.17">1Sam 10:17</reference>. It was deemed a sacred place among the Israelites; for we find, from 1 Maccabees 3:46, that the Jews assembled here to seek God, when their enemies were in possession of the temple.
entries.1285728b605dae7c5ba9f4e868e2d31dfb65fbae: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen8094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8095" type="x-p"/> And Zelah - This was the burying-place of Saul, Jonathan, and the family of Kish. See <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.14">2Sam 21:14</reference>. <div eID="gen8095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8096" type="x-p"/> Jebusi, which is Jerusalem - We often meet with this name, and it is evident that it was the ancient name of Jerusalem, which was also called Salem; and was probably the place in which Melchizedek reigned in the days of Abraham; though some think a different place is meant; for that there was another place of the same name, is evident from <reference osisRef="Joh.3.23">Joh 3:23</reference>. This place, called Salim by the evangelist, is said to be near to Enon, and there John baptized, because there was much water in the place. This, however, must not be confounded with the Salem mentioned above; for that this was a name of Jerusalem, is evident from <reference osisRef="Psa.76.1">Psa 76:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.76.2">Psa 76:2</reference> : In Judah is God known: his name is great in Israel. In Salem also is his tabernacle, and his dwelling-place in Zion. This must refer to Jerusalem, where the temple was situated. Whether Jebus or Jebusi had its name from the Jebusites, or the Jebusites from it, cannot be ascertained.  <chapter eID="Josh.18"/> <div eID="gen8096" type="x-p"/>

entries.87af6eceeea14e091eab57bb1dd79ab1b61febaa: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.1">Jos 18:1</reference> <div eID="gen2915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2916" type="x-p"/> The Tabernacle Set Up at Shiloh. - As soon as the tribe of Ephraim had received its inheritance, Joshua commanded the whole congregation to assemble in Shiloh, and there set up the tabernacle, in order that, as the land was conquered, the worship of Jehovah might henceforth be regularly observed in accordance with the law. The selection of Shiloh as the site for the sanctuary was hardly occasioned by the fitness of the place for this purpose, on account of its being situated upon a mountain in the centre of the land, for there were many other places that would have been quite as suitable in this respect; the reason is rather to be found in the name of the place, viz., <hi type="italic">Shiloh</hi>, i.e., rest, which called to mind the promised Shiloh (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>), and therefore appeared to be pre-eminently suitable to be the resting-place of the sanctuary of the Lord, where His name was to dwell in Israel, until He should come who was to give true rest to His people as the Prince of Peace. In any case, however, Joshua did not follow his own judgment in selecting Shiloh for this purpose, but acted in simple accordance with the instructions of God, as the Lord had expressly reserved to himself the choice of the place where His name should dwell (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.11">Deu 12:11</reference>). <hi type="italic">Shiloh</hi>, according to the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi>, was twelve Roman miles or five hours to the south of Neapolis (Nablus), and about eight hours to the north of Jerusalem; at present it is a heap of ruins, bearing the name of <hi type="italic">Seilun</hi> (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. p. 85). The tabernacle continued standing at Shiloh during the time of the judges, until the ark of the covenant fell into the hands of the Philistines, in the lifetime of Eli, when the holy tent was robbed of its soul, and reduced to the mere shadow of a sanctuary. After this it was removed to Nob (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.2">1Sa 21:2</reference>); but in consequence of the massacre inflicted by Saul upon the inhabitants of this place (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.19">1Sa 22:19</reference>), it was taken to Gibeon (1Ki 3:4 : see <hi type="italic">Keil</hi>, Bibl. Arch. i. §22). From this time forward Shilloh continued to decline, because the Lord had rejected it (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.60">Psa 78:60</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.12">Jer 7:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.26.6">Jer 26:6</reference>). That it was destroyed by the Assyrians, as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> affirms, is not stated in the history.
entries.938b195d22c5cf417c312b1cf1db8ba014057c51: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.2">Jos 18:2</reference> <div eID="gen2916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2917" type="x-p"/> Survey of the Land that had yet to be Divided. - Jos 18:2. After the tabernacle had been set up, the casting of the lots and division of the land among the other seven tribes were to be continued; namely at Shiloh, to which the congregation had removed with the sanctuary.
entries.82a2a934c771b08a3ef995089d1f76cb56a67dcb: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.3-Josh.18.4">Jos 18:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen2917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2918" type="x-p"/> But, for the reasons explained in <reference osisRef="Josh.14.1">Jos 14:1</reference>, these tribes showed themselves “<hi type="italic">slack to go to possess the land which the Lord had given them</hi>,” i.e., not merely to conquer it, but to have it divided by lot, and to enter in and take possession. Joshua charged them with this, and directed them to appoint three men for each of the seven tribes, that they might be sent out to go through the land, and describe it according to the measure of their inheritance. “<hi type="italic">According to their inheritance</hi>,” i.e., with special reference to the fact that seven tribes were to receive it for their inheritance. The description was not a formal measurement, although the art of surveying was well known in Egypt in ancient times, and was regularly carried out after the annual inundations of the Nile (<hi type="italic">Herod.</hi> ii. 109; <hi type="italic">Strabo</hi>, xvii. 787; <hi type="italic">Diod. Sic.</hi> i. 69); so that the Israelites might have learned it there. But כּתב does not mean to measure; and it was not a formal measurement that was required, for the purpose of dividing the land that yet remained into seven districts, since the tribes differed in numerical strength, and therefore the boundaries of the territory assigned them could not be settled till after the lots had been cast. The meaning of the word is to describe; and according to <reference osisRef="Josh.18.9">Jos 18:9</reference>, it was chiefly to the towns that reference was made: so that the description required by Joshua in all probability consisted simply in the preparation of lists of the towns in the different parts of the land, with an account of their size and character; also with “notices of the quality and condition of the soil; what lands were fertile, and what they produced; where the country was mountainous, and where it was level; which lands were well watered, and which were dry; and any other things that would indicate the character of the soil, and facilitate a comparison between the different parts of the land” (<hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi>). The reasons which induced Joshua to take steps for the first time now for securing a survey of the land, are given in Jos 14:1. The men chosen for the purpose were able to carry out their task without receiving any hindrance from the Canaanites. For whilst the latter were crushed, if not exterminated, by the victories which the Israelites had gained, it was not necessary for the twenty-one Israelitish men to penetrate into every corner of the land, and every town that was still inhabited by the Canaanites, in order to accomplish their end.
entries.e86199802af256ed0769efde4635b6ce852b0110: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.5-Josh.18.6">Jos 18:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen2918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2919" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And divide it into seven parts</hi>,” viz., for the purpose of casting lots. Judah, however, was still to remain in its land to the south, and Ephraim in its territory to the north. The seven portions thus obtained they were to bring to Joshua, that he might then cast the lot for the seven tribes “before the Lord,” i.e., before the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.51">Jos 19:51</reference>).
entries.e19159c23f735f893f7b383465bfcba90a5c36f9: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.7">Jos 18:7</reference> <div eID="gen2919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2920" type="x-p"/> There were only seven tribes that had still to receive their portions; for the tribe of Levi was to receive no portion in the land (vid., Josh 13-14), and Gad, Reuben, and half Manasseh had received their inheritance already on the other side of the Jordan.
entries.26ecf6ee05cb76b8fae5cf35d44d2b8069dc6018: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.8-Josh.18.9">Jos 18:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen2920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2921" type="x-p"/> Execution of this command.
entries.eb65e84ab9d6014db866f2b6122225e601702846: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.10">Jos 18:10</reference> <div eID="gen2921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2922" type="x-p"/> Joshua finishes the casting of the lots at Shiloh. <div eID="gen2922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2923" type="x-p"/> Inheritance of the Tribe of Benjamin. - <reference osisRef="Josh.18.11">Jos 18:11</reference>-20. <hi type="italic">Boundaries</hi> of the inheritance. - Jos 18:11. The territory of their lot (i.e., the territory assigned to the Benjaminites by lot) came out (through the falling out of the lot) between the sons of Judah and the sons of Joseph.
entries.87147a4b9cb08041759f41cd8f2b312e99e85688: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.12-Josh.18.14">Jos 18:12-14</reference> <div eID="gen2923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2924" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">northern boundary</hi> (“the boundary towards the north side”) therefore coincided with the southern boundary of Ephraim as far as Lower Beth-horon, and has already been commented upon in the exposition of <reference osisRef="Josh.16.1">Jos 16:1</reference>-3. The <hi type="italic">western boundary</hi> follows in Jos 18:14. At Beth-horon the boundary curved round and turned southwards on the western side, namely from the mountain before (in front of) Beth-horon southwards; and “<hi type="italic">the going out thereof were at Kirjath-baal, which is Kirjath-jearim</hi>,” the town of the Judaeans mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.60">Jos 15:60</reference>, the present <hi type="italic">Kureyet el Enab</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.9.17">Jos 9:17</reference>).
entries.e05f4b3df74916d99673ba8a0cd58ab4e3642ec2: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.15-Josh.18.19">Jos 18:15-19</reference> <div eID="gen2924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2925" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">As for the southern boundary from the end of Kirjath-jearim onwards, the</hi> (southern) <hi type="italic">boundary went out on the west</hi> (i.e., it started from the west), <hi type="italic">and went out</hi> (terminated) <hi type="italic">at the fountain of the water of Nephtoah</hi>.” Consequently it coincided with the northern boundary of Judah, as described in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.5-Josh.15.9">Jos 15:5-9</reference>, except that it is given there from east to west, and here from west to east (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.5-Josh.15.9">Jos 15:5-9</reference>). In the construction haגּבוּל תּוצאותיו, the noun הגּבוּל is in apposition to the suffix: the outgoings of it, namely of the border (see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §291, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.).
entries.3aa761e1d1b769d0e06584dc22cc0f0bfed66d15: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.20">Jos 18:20</reference> <div eID="gen2925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2926" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">eastern boundary</hi> was the Jordan.
entries.c60cf76330015db09d2e0a9ea8ab65e3bc19821f: <reference osisRef="Josh.18.21-Josh.18.28">Jos 18:21-28</reference> <div eID="gen2926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2927" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">towns</hi> of Benjamin are divided into two groups. The <hi type="italic">first</hi> group (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.21-Josh.18.24">Jos 18:21-24</reference>) contains twelve towns in the eastern portion of the territory. <hi type="italic">Jericho</hi>: the present <hi type="italic">Riha</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.2.1">Jos 2:1</reference>). <hi type="italic">Beth-hoglah</hi>, now <hi type="italic">Ain Hajla</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Josh.15.6">Jos 15:6</reference>). <hi type="italic">Emek-keziz</hi>: the name has been preserved in the Wady <hi type="italic">el Kaziz</hi>, on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho, on the south-east of the Apostle’s Well (see <hi type="italic">Van de Velde</hi>, Mem. p. 328).

entries.c105137f981bd022f62dabade2db564baf3a5f9f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.18.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Josh.18.1" sID="gen24137" type="section"/> <div sID="gen24138" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">And the whole congregation of the children of Israel,</hi> etc Here we have a narrative of the celebrated convention held in Shiloh, where it was deliberated, as to the casting of the remaining lots. For although with pious zeal they had attempted the casting of lots, yet the proceeding had been interrupted, as if victory behooved to precede the distribution which depended solely on the mouth of God. They assemble, therefore, in Shiloh to determine what was necessary to be done in future. And there is no doubt that Joshua summoned this meeting in order to raise them from their lethargy. For they do not come forward spontaneously with any proposal, but he begins with upbraiding them with having been sluggish and remiss in entering on the inheritance which God had bestowed upon them. It is easy to infer from his speech that they had shown great alacrity at the outset, but that there had been no perseverance.<div eID="gen24138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24139" type="x-p"/>And yet that obedience, which shortly after grew languid, was honored with the approbation of the Holy Spirit. It is to be observed that the people are blamed, not for neglecting to proceed to the lot, but for not occupying the inheritance divinely offered to them. And, certainly, as the distribution by lot was a sign of confidence, so each district which fell out to each was a sure and faithful pledge of future possession; for the Lord was by no means deluding them in assigning to each his portion.<div eID="gen24139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24140" type="x-p"/>The word <foreign xml:lang="he">דפה</foreign>, which I have translated “to cease,” signifies also to be remiss or feeble. He charges them, therefore, with base heartlessness, in that while the full time for routing the enemy had arrived, they by their delays retard and suspend the effect of the divine goodness. For had they been contented with the bare lot, and faithfully embraced the results which it gave, they would doubtless have been prompt and expeditious in carrying on the war, nay, would have hastened like conquerors to a triumph.<div eID="gen24140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24141" type="x-p"/>The ark is said to have been stationed at Shiloh, <note n="161"> <div sID="gen24142" type="x-p"/> This place, which afterwards became so celebrated as the fixed station of the ark and tabernacle during the remainder of Joshua’s life and the rule of the Judges, down to the tragical death of Eli, is described in <reference osisRef="Bible:Judg.21.19">Judges 21:19</reference>, as “On the north side of Bethel, on the east side of the highway that goeth up from Bethel to Shechem, and on the south of Lebonah.” This minute description corresponds with a place now called Seilun, which is situated about twenty miles N.N.E. from Jerusalem, and has several ruins indicative of an ancient site. If this was the place, it stood nearly in the center of the country, and was thus the most convenient which could have been selected. While its locality made it easily accessible from all quarters, its site, in the heart of a basin completely enclosed by hills except on the south, where a narrow valley opens into a plain, admirably adapted it for the still and solemn performance of religious services. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen24142" type="x-p"/> </note> not only that the consultation might be graver and more sacred, as held in the presence of God, but because it was a completely subjugated place, and safe from all external violence and injury. For it behooved to be their special care to prevent its exposure to sudden assault. No doubt the hand of God would have been stretched to ward off attacks of the enemy from any quarter; still, however, though God dwelt among them, they were to be regarded as its guardians and attendants.<div eID="gen24141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24143" type="x-p"/>But although a station for the ark was then chosen, it was not a perpetual abode, but only a temporary lodging. For it was not left to the will or suffrages of the people to fix the seat where God should dwell, but they behooved to wait for the period so often referred to in the Law, when he was to establish the memorial of his name elsewhere. This was at length accomplished when Mount Zion was set apart for the Temple. For this reason it is said in the Psalm,<div eID="gen24143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24144" type="x-p"/>“Our feet shall stand within thy gates, O Jerusalem.”<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.122.2">Psalm 122:2</reference>)<div eID="gen24144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24145" type="x-p"/>These words intimate that up to that time the ark was pilgrimating. At last the ruin and devastation of Shiloh showed that no rank or dignity can screen those who corrupt the blessings of God from his vengeance. Up to the death of Eli, God allowed his sacred name to be worshipped there; but when all religion was polluted by the impiety of the priests, and almost abolished by the ingratitude of the people, that spot became to posterity a signal monument of punishment. Accordingly, Jeremiah tells the inhabitants of Jerusalem, who were proudly boasting of their Temple, to turn their eyes to that example. Speaking in the name of the Lord, he says,<div eID="gen24145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24146" type="x-p"/>“Go you now unto my place which was in Shiloh, where I set my name at the first, and see what I did to it for the wickedness of my people Israel.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.7.12">Jeremiah 7:12</reference>)<div eID="gen24146" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.18.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen24137" osisID="Josh.18.1" type="section"/>
entries.b25827da567ca90b112fc1901c0ba3c23af2664d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.18.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Josh.18.4" sID="gen24147" type="section"/> <div sID="gen24148" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4.</hi> <hi type="italic">Give out from among you three men, </hi>etc Caleb and Joshua had already surveyed those regions, and the people had learned much by inquiry: Joshua, however, wishes the land to be divided as if according to actual survey <note n="162"> <div sID="gen24149" type="x-p"/> Latin, “<foreign xml:lang="la">Quasi ex praesenti aspectu</foreign>.” French, “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Comme s’ils eussent este presens sur le lieu</foreign>;” “As if they had been present on the spot.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen24149" type="x-p"/> </note> and orders three surveyors to be appointed for each of the seven tribes, in order that by the mouth of two or three persons every dispute may be settled. But nothing seems more incongruous than to send twenty-one men, who were not only to pass directly through a hostile country, but to trace it through all its various windings and turnings, so as not to leave a single corner unexamined, to calculate, its length and breadth, and even make due allowance for its inequalities. Every person whom they happened to meet must readily have suspected who they were, and for what reason they had been employed on this expedition. In short, no free return lay open for them except through a thousand deaths. Assuredly they would not have encountered so much danger from blind and irrational impulse, nor would Joshua have exposed them to such manifest danger had they not been aware that all those nations, struck with terror from heaven, desired nothing so much as peace. For although they hated the children of Israel, still, having been subdued by so many overthrows, they did not dare to move a finger against them, and thus the surveyors proceeded in safety as through a peaceful territory, under the pretext either of trading, or at least of making a harmless visit. <note n="163"> <div sID="gen24150" type="x-p"/> Latin, “<foreign xml:lang="la">Innoxii hospites</foreign>.” French, “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Estrangers innocens qui passent leur chemin</foreign>;” “Innocent strangers passing on their way.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen24150" type="x-p"/> </note> It is also possible that they arranged themselves in different parties, and thus made the journey more secretly. It is certain, indeed, that there was only one source from which they could have derived all this courage and confidence, from trusting under the shadow of the wings of the Almighty, and thus having no fear of blind and stupid men. Hence the praise here bestowed on their ready will. For had they not been persuaded that the hands of those nations were tied up by supernal power, they would have had a just and honest cause for refusing. <note n="164"> <div sID="gen24151" type="x-p"/> These observations are made on the understanding that the survey made on this occasion was very minute, embracing, as Calvin here expresses it, all the “various windings and turnings,” so as not to leave a single corner unexamined, and extending with the same minuteness, not only to the lands actually conquered, but to those still in the undisputed possession of the original inhabitants. Assuming this to be the fact, the dangers to be encountered by the surveyors are certainly not exaggerated in the very graphical description of them here given, and nothing but a series of miraculous interposition’s could have saved them. It may be suggested, however, that the object of the surveyors was only to obtain such a general measurement as might suffice, in the manner already explained, for the taking of the lot, and that such a measurement might possibly have been made without much danger of awakening the suspicion, or rousing the hostility of the actual inhabitants. That the survey was more cursory than minute seems to be indicated by the description given of it in <reference osisRef="Bible:Josh.18.9">Joshua 18:9</reference>, “And the men went and passed through the land, and described it by cities.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen24151" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen24148" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Josh.18.4" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen24147" osisID="Josh.18.4" type="section"/>

And the men went and passed, etc Here not only is praise bestowed on the ready obedience by which their virtue shone forth conspicuous, but the Lord gives a signal manifestation of his favor by deigning to bestow remarkable success on pious Joshua and the zeal of the people. Had they crept along by subterranean burrows, they could scarcely have escaped innumerable dangers, but now, when they are taking notes of the cities and their sites, of the fields, the varying features of the districts, and all the coasts, and without meeting with any adverse occurrence, return in safety to their countrymen, who can doubt that their life had been kept safe among a thousand deaths by a wonderful exertion of divine power? It is accordingly said emphatically, that they returned to celebrate the grace of God, which is just equivalent to saying that they were brought back by the hand of God. This made the people proceed more willingly to the casting of lots. For their minds would not yet have been well purged of fastidiousness had they not perceived in that journey a signal display of divine favor, promising them that the final issue would be according to their wish. Joshua is hence said to have divided according to the inheritance of each, as if he were sending them to enter on a quiet possession, though the effect depended on the divine presence, because it ought to have been enough for them that the whole business was carried on by the authority of God, who never deceives his people, even when he seems to sport with them. In what sense the ark of the covenant is called God, or the face of God, I have already explained in many passages.

In the lot of Benjamin nothing occurs particularly deserving of notice, unless that a small tribe takes precedence of the others. I admit, indeed, that its limits were narrowed in proportion to the fewness of its numbers, because it obtained only twenty-six cities; but still an honor was bestowed upon it in the mere circumstance of its receiving its inheritance before more distinguished tribes. We may add, that in this way they were conjoined and made neighbors to the other
Latin, “Reliquis filiis.” French, “Des autres enfans;” “The other children,” — an apparent oversight, as if Benjamin had been a son and not a brother of Joseph. — Ed.
children of Joseph, with whom their relationship was more immediate. For they were placed in the middle between the children of Ephraim and Manasseh on the one side, and those of Judah on the other. They had also the distinguished honor of including Jerusalem in their inheritance, though they afterwards granted it by a kind of precarious tenure to the children of Judah for a royal residence.
Latin, “Postea filiis Juda quasi precario sedem regiam concederent.” French, “Depuis ils la baillerent aux enfans de Juda comme par emprunt, pour en faire le siege royal;” “Afterwards they let it to the children of Judah as by loan, to make it the royal residence.” These words seem to imply that at some time or other a regular agreement to this effect had been made, but we nowhere find any mention of such an agreement. It would rather seem from Joshua 15:63, and Judges 1:8, 21, that the inhabitants of Judah possessed Jerusalem in consequence of their having wrested it from the Jebusites. — Ed.
It is strange, however, that having obtained such a quiet locality, they did not live on peaceful and friendly terms with their neighbors. But we possess the prophecy of Jacob,
“Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf; in the morning he shall devour the prey, and at night he shall divide the spoil.” (Genesis 49:27)
They must, therefore, have been by nature of a covetous and turbulent disposition, or from some necessity not now known to us, they must have been impelled to live upon plunder. In regard to the city of Luz, the other name is added, (“the same is Bethel,”) because then only did the name given by Jacob come into common use. (Genesis 28:19) It was at no great distance from Beth-Aven, whose name, as it was opprobrious and infamous, was transferred to Bethel itself, after it was corrupted and polluted by impious superstitions.
This refers to the setting up of the golden calves by Jeroboam, and the idolatrous worship which thus impiously originated by him was long practiced by his successors. See 1 Kings 12:28-33; 1 Kings 13; 2 Kings 10:29-31; 2 Kings 23:15; Amos 4:4; Amos 5:4-6; Hosea 4:15; Hosea 10:5,8. Bethel or “the house of God,” so called by Jacob the morning after he had risen from his wonderful vision, having forfeited its name in consequence of the abominations practiced at it, became afterwards known by that of Bethaven, “the house of idols,” or of vanity and iniquity. — Ed.
It is probable that Ciriath-Baal was called Ciriath-Jeharim, to take away the name of the idol, which would have been a stain on its true piety. For it certainly would have been base and shameful that the lips of the people should have been polluted by the name of a protector who was an enemy to the true God.

                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And there remained among the children of Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rael seven tribes, which had not yet received their inheritance.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And Joshua said unto the children of Israel, How long are ye slack to go to possess the land <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">This slackness is supposed to arise, partly from their dissa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tisfaction in the portions already allotted, <ns0:hi>Iudahs</ns0:hi> being too large, as it appeared; and <ns0:hi>Iosephs</ns0:hi> too narrow, as they com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plained; partly from an opinion of the impossibility of ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />king any regular and equal distribution of the Parts, till the Whole were better known, and more exactly Surveyed, which accordingly is here done; and partly, because being weary of War, and having sufficient plenty of all things in their pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent condition, they grew slothful and secure, and were un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />willing to run into new Hazards and Wars, as they perceived by <ns0:hi>Ioshua's</ns0:hi> answer to the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Ioseph, Ios.</ns0:hi> 17. 15, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> they were likely to do when they entred upon their several Possessions.</ns0:note> which the LORD God of your fathers hath gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven you?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Give out from among you three men <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Three, not One, for more exact observation both of the measure and quality of the several Portions, and for grea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter assurance and evidence of their care and faithfulness in giving in their Account.</ns0:note> of <ns0:hi>each</ns0:hi> tribe <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Either One of each of these Tribes, who were yet unprovided for; or rather Two of all the Tribes, even of them who had already received their Portions; which was highly expedient, that in case it should appear that there was not a sufficiency for each of these Tribes who wanted their Portions, their Brethren might be more ready either to assist them in procuring more Land, or to part with some of their own Portion to them.</ns0:note>: and I will send them, and they shall rise, and go thorow the land <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which they might now safely do, because the Terror of the late War was yet upon the <ns0:hi>Canaanites,</ns0:hi> who were loath to rouse so near and potent an Enemy.</ns0:note>, and describe it ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to the inheritance of them, and they shall come <ns0:hi>again</ns0:hi> to me.</ns0:p>
